questions.q: State the SI unit of power and write the formula for average power in terms of work and time.
questions.a: The SI unit of power is the watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J/s. Average power is given by P_avg = W / t, where W is work done (J) and t is time interval (s). A wrong answer (e.g., giving unit as joule or newton) reveals confusion between work and power, or missing the time aspect of power.

questions.q: A constant force of 10 N acts on a block moving at a constant velocity of 2 m/s in the direction of the force. What is the instantaneous power delivered by the force? Explain why this equals the average power over any interval.
questions.a: Instantaneous power P = F·v = (10 N)(2 m/s) = 20 W. Since both force and velocity are constant, the work done in any interval Δt is W = F·v Δt, so average power = W/Δt = F·v = 20 W, same as instantaneous. A student who says "average power is different" misunderstands that constancy of F and v makes the rate of work uniform.

questions.q: A particle of mass 2 kg moves along the x-axis such that its velocity varies with time as v(t) = 3t^2 m/s. A net force F(t) = 12t N acts on it in the direction of motion. Calculate the instantaneous power at t = 2 s.
questions.a: At t = 2 s, v = 3(2)^2 = 12 m/s, F = 12(2) = 24 N. Instantaneous power P = F·v = (24 N)(12 m/s) = 288 W. Unit check: N·m/s = J/s = W. A wrong answer (e.g., using average force or velocity) shows the student does not grasp that instantaneous power uses values at a specific instant.

questions.q: A force F = (3i + 4j) N acts on a particle moving with velocity v = (2i - 1j) m/s. Compute the instantaneous power. Is the kinetic energy increasing or decreasing at this instant?
questions.a: P = F·v = (3)(2) + (4)(-1) = 6 - 4 = 2 W. Since P > 0, kinetic energy is increasing (dK/dt = P > 0). A student who computes magnitude of force times magnitude of velocity (5 × √5 ≈ 11.2 W) ignores the dot product and the angle between vectors, a common vector algebra error.

questions.q: A student claims: "If a car engine delivers a constant power of 50 kW, the force exerted by the engine on the car is constant at all speeds." Evaluate this statement.
questions.a: The statement is false. For constant power P, force F = P/v. As speed v increases, force F must decrease to keep P constant. At low speeds, the force is large; at high speeds, it is small. A student who agrees confuses constant power with constant force, not understanding the inverse relationship between force and velocity for constant power.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a spring balance, a trolley, and a stopwatch to estimate the average power you exert while pulling the trolley horizontally at constant speed over a distance of 5 m. List the measurements needed and the formula you would use.
questions.a: Measure the constant pulling force F (spring balance reading in N), the time t taken to cover 5 m (stopwatch), and verify constant speed. Average power = Work/time = (F × 5 m) / t. A good answer includes checking that the force is horizontal and speed is constant (so net force zero, applied force equals friction). A poor answer omits the need for constant speed or forgets to multiply force by distance.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Average power is the total work done divided by the total time interval over which the work is performed, while instantaneous power is the limiting value of average power as the time interval ______ zero, equal to the dot product of the net force acting on a body and its instantaneous velocity (P = F·v).
Fill in the blank: Observe a ceiling fan starting from rest: ______ it takes large force to overcome inertia, but once at constant speed, the motor only balances friction.
What is Average power? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Average power is the total work done divided by the total time interval over which the work is performed, while instantaneous power is the limiting value of average power as the time interval approaches zero, equal to the dot product of the net force acting on a body and its instantaneous velocity (P = F·v).

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Ask: "What if the force or velocity changes during the motion?" Introduce the limit Δt → ______ to define instantaneous power.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Average power?
questions.a: Students often think instantaneous power is just "average power over a very small time" and try to compute it by dividing work done in a small Δt by that Δt without taking the limit.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to distinguish between average and instantaneous power in a given physical situation, calculate instantaneous power using P = F·v for a force and velocity at a specific instant, and compute average power from work-energy data over a finite interval.
